subtitle: Practice the craft of delegating: deciding what to hand over, naming how much authority goes with it, offering stretch work openly, and coaching through difficulty without taking the work back.
audience: For first-year and experienced supervisors, and for leads who hand work to others, who want to delegate with clear authority and support and make sure the growth that delegated work brings reaches the whole team.

lessons.title: Delegation as a leadership duty, not a favor
objectives: Explain delegation as handing over a task together with the authority and support needed to complete it.
Sort your current work into what needs your role, what others could do now and what others could learn to do.
Identify two costs to the team when a leader keeps most of the work.
Describe where your own default about doing work yourself came from and how it affects others.
lessons.teaching:
Delegation is part of the job of leading, not a favor you do when you are busy. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's 2015 federal managerial framework describes delegation as empowering employees by assigning tasks and granting the authority that goes with them, then providing resources and timely, objective feedback on the work. That definition holds three duties together: the task, the authority and the support. Handing over a task without the other two is not delegation. It asks someone to carry work they cannot fully move.

Start by sorting your own work. Some work should stay with you: decisions that need your role, such as performance matters and anything you handle with Human Resources or labor relations, along with confidential matters and commitments only you can make for the team. Much of the rest can be handed over or shared, including recurring tasks you mastered long ago, analysis others could do with some support, and parts of larger projects that would help someone grow. A useful test is to ask what someone could do now, what they could learn to do, and what truly needs you.

Doing it all yourself has costs that are easy to miss. The work slows when everything waits for you. Knowledge about how things get done sits with one person, which leaves the team fragile when you are away. People who could grow stay where they are, and they notice. Ask yourself where you learned that doing the work yourself is the responsible choice. Many leaders were rewarded early in their careers for being the one who always delivered, and that habit can follow them into a role where it holds others back.

Delegation also shapes who gets seen. When a supervisor holds the visible work and hands out only routine tasks, the team's skills stay hidden from the people who make later decisions. Before you decide what to keep, ask who is affected, whose experience of the work you might be missing and how you would find out. A short conversation with each person about the work they want to learn often shows options you had not considered. Then decide, and check after a few weeks whether the change made the work better for the people it touches.
lessons.keyPoint: Delegation hands over a task together with the authority and support to complete it. Keep what truly needs your role, share the rest on purpose, and notice what doing it all yourself costs the team.
lessons.example: Practice case: Marisol supervises a licensing team in disability services. Since her promotion she still reviews every provider renewal file herself before it goes out, because she knows the rules well and mistakes are costly. Files now wait a week for her. Ahmed, a licensing consultant with six years on the team, has asked twice to take on final reviews for simpler renewals. Grace, who joined last year, has said she would like to learn the review process. Marisol has an hour free on Friday.
lessons.question: What should Marisol do with her Friday hour?
choices: Meet with Ahmed and Grace to agree which renewals Ahmed can finalize, what Grace will learn first, and when they will check in.
Use the hour to clear the backlog herself, then return to delegation once the files are current and the team's pressure has eased.
Ask Ahmed to take over all final reviews starting Monday so the files move, and tell him to bring her any questions.
feedback: This matches the task to experience, gives Ahmed real authority for a defined set of files and starts Grace's learning. A planned check-in keeps quality visible.
Clearing the backlog feels responsible, but the pattern that created it stays. Ahmed and Grace keep waiting, and the next backlog arrives with no one else ready.
This moves the files, but it hands over everything at once with no agreed limits or check-in. Ahmed carries the risk alone, and Grace's interest goes unanswered.
lessons.reflection: Which part of your work do you keep because only you can do it, and which part do you keep because it feels safer or faster to do it yourself?
lessons.action: This week, list the recurring tasks you did yourself over the past two weeks. Mark each one as needs my role, someone could do now, or someone could learn. Choose one task from the last two groups to hand over.

check.question: According to the federal managerial framework in this lesson, what turns handing over a task into delegation?
check.correct: The person also receives the authority to act and the support needed to finish.
wrong: The task is written up with a clear deadline before it is assigned to anyone else.
The task goes to the most experienced person so that the result is reliable.
check.feedback: Delegation holds the task, the authority and the support together. A deadline and an experienced person can help, but without authority and support the person cannot fully move the work.

lessons.title: Matching the task, the person and the authority
objectives: Choose a level of authority for a task based on its risk and the person's experience with similar work.
State the outcome, the limits and the check-in points when you hand over a piece of work.
Distinguish a decision the person can make from one that still needs your approval or another area's.
Adapt how you hand over and follow up so the person can take part fully.
lessons.teaching:
Delegation is not all or nothing. Between doing a task yourself and handing it over completely, there are several useful levels. The person can look into something and report back. They can recommend a course and you decide. They can decide and tell you before acting. They can decide and act, then update you at the next check-in. Or they can own the work fully. Naming the level out loud prevents the most common delegation problem: two people with different ideas about who decides.

Match the level to the task and to the person's experience with similar work. A task with high risk to people served, a legal deadline or public attention may start at a lower level even for an experienced colleague, with the level rising as the work goes well. A task someone has done many times can move straight to full ownership. Base the choice on what the person has done and what the task demands, not on a general impression of their confidence or polish. Impressions like that often reflect how closely someone's style matches your own.

Be clear about the outcome, the limits and the check-ins when you hand work over. The outcome is what done looks like and who it serves. The limits: the budget, policy and timelines that apply, who else must approve, and anything that must not change. The check-ins: when you will talk, in what form, and what should prompt an earlier conversation. If an assignment would have someone perform substantially all the duties of a temporarily unoccupied position in a different classification, talk with Human Resources first. Minnesota Management and Budget's procedure on work out of class assignments sets rules for those arrangements, and labor agreement terms apply.

Ask how the person works best, and adapt the handover to fit. Some people want the brief in writing so they can return to it, some prefer to talk it through, and some need materials in an accessible format or captioned meetings. Ask rather than assume what someone needs. If a request touches an accommodation, follow your agency's accommodation process with Human Resources. After the first check-in, ask what was unclear and change how you brief the next piece of work.
lessons.keyPoint: Say out loud how much authority goes with the work. Match that level to the task's risk and the person's experience, and agree on the outcome, the limits and the check-ins before the work begins.
lessons.example: Practice case: Tomasz, a policy lead in an economic assistance area, asks Jalen, an analyst, to prepare options for changing a county reporting form. Jalen has done similar analysis but has never presented to county partners. Tomasz says only, "Take the lead on this." Two weeks later Jalen shares a recommended form with Rosa, a county partner, who assumes it is final. Tomasz had expected to review options first. Rosa's team has started planning around the new form.
lessons.question: What should Tomasz do now?
choices: Email Rosa that the form is not final, then tell Jalen he will handle all county conversations from here so there is no more confusion.
Let the form stand, since Jalen acted in good faith and reversing it would embarrass him, and plan to be clearer next time.
Own the unclear handover with Jalen, agree on a level for the rest of the work, and contact Rosa together about what is still open.
feedback: Correcting the record matters, but taking the county work back tells Jalen the problem was his, when the authority was never named. He loses the chance to finish well.
This spares a hard moment, but it commits the area to a form no one decided on, and Rosa's team keeps planning around a choice that may still change.
This names the real cause, sets a clear level for what remains and keeps Jalen in the partner relationship. Rosa hears one consistent account of what is open.
lessons.reflection: Think of the last time you asked someone to take the lead on something. How much authority did you mean, and how would they have known?
lessons.action: Before you next hand over a piece of work, write three lines: what done looks like, the limits that apply and when you will check in. Add the level of authority in plain words and share it with the person.

check.question: A task carries a legal deadline and the colleague taking it is very experienced. What does this lesson suggest about the level of authority?
check.correct: Start at a level that fits the risk, then raise it as the work goes well.
wrong: Give full ownership at once, since experience matters more than the task's risk.
Keep the task yourself, since high-risk work should not be delegated to others.
check.feedback: The level depends on both the task and the person's experience. High-risk work can still be delegated, often with more frequent check-ins at first, and the authority can grow as the work goes well.

lessons.title: Delegation as development: offering stretch work
objectives: Plan a stretch assignment that names the skill it builds, the criteria for taking it on and the support that comes with it.
Compare how a habit of giving work to whoever is ready looks at different points on the intercultural continuum.
Explain how readiness for stretch work can reflect who received earlier chances.
Draft an offer of delegated work that names its starting level of authority and lets people respond in more than one way.
lessons.teaching:
Delegated work is one of the main ways people grow on the job. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's 2015 report on learning for leaders describes a developmental assignment as one designed to stretch a person beyond their existing skills. The Center for Creative Leadership's research on how managers and executives learn found challenging assignments to be a main source of growth; its 70-20-10 guideline is a rule of thumb, not a measured law. OPM's managerial framework adds that tasks should be delegated on objective criteria such as skill, experience, developmental needs and interests, workload and fairness.

Ask yourself who usually gets your stretch work, and who has never been offered it. Then ask why those people come to mind first. The answer is rarely about intent. Stretch work tends to go to the person who asks first, who works most like the leader or who already did something similar. Each assignment then builds the experience that makes that person look ready next time, while others wait for a chance they were never given.

The intercultural development continuum described by IDI, LLC can help you examine how you offer stretch work, as a practice and never as a trait of any person. A Minimization habit sounds fair: I give stretch work to whoever is ready, and I treat everyone the same. An Acceptance habit notices that readiness often reflects who got earlier chances, and that people show interest differently, some by asking directly and some by waiting to be invited. An Adaptation habit changes the practice: describing the work openly, naming criteria, offering support that lets someone without the earlier chance succeed, and asking people who have not raised their hands.

Make the offer specific: the work, the skill it builds, what it takes and the support that comes with it. Support might mean regular check-ins, a more experienced colleague to consult or time freed from other duties. Name the starting level of authority and what would let it grow, so the person knows what they will actually decide. Let people respond in writing or in conversation. Washington State's enterprise leadership competencies, written for that state's leaders, describe inclusive leaders as giving every employee the chance to develop their skills. That is a fair standard to hold yourself to, whatever the size of your team.
lessons.keyPoint: Readiness for stretch work is often built by earlier chances. Offer delegated work openly, with clear criteria and real support, so that development reaches people who have not been offered it before.
lessons.example: Practice case: Priya supervises a waiver program team in disability services that supports lead agencies. A new training series for lead agency staff needs someone to design and deliver it. Kwame has led the last three trainings and is eager to lead again. Nora, a program consultant who knows the policy deeply, has never been asked to train and has not volunteered. Luis, hired eight months ago, said in a recent one-to-one that he wants presenting experience.
lessons.question: How should Priya decide who leads the training series?
choices: Give it to Kwame, who has shown he can do it well, and ask him to include Nora and Luis as helpers on one session each.
Describe the work and its support to the whole team, invite interest in writing or in person, and consider a shared lead with coaching.
Assign it to Nora because she has never had the chance, and tell the team it is her turn so that the decision feels fair to everyone involved.
feedback: This keeps quality steady and adds some exposure, but Kwame keeps the visible role and the others stay helpers. The pattern of who leads continues for another cycle.
This makes the offer visible, lets people respond in a way that suits them and builds in support, so the choice rests on interest, criteria and development.
This corrects the pattern with good intent, but it decides for Nora without asking about her interest, and calling it her turn makes development sound like a rotation.
lessons.reflection: When you hand out work that would help someone grow, what usually makes a person come to mind first, and how might others show interest in ways you miss?
lessons.action: Choose one upcoming piece of work that could stretch someone. Write two sentences on the skill it builds, the support that comes with it and the starting level of authority, and share them with your whole team before you decide who takes it.

check.question: Which response reflects an Adaptation habit in offering stretch work?
check.correct: Changing how the work is offered and supported so more people can take it on.
wrong: Giving the work to whoever shows readiness first, so everyone is treated alike.
Noticing that readiness can reflect earlier chances, then choosing the usual person.
check.feedback: Treating everyone the same is a Minimization habit, and noticing the role of earlier chances is the start of Acceptance. Adaptation changes the practice itself: the offer, the criteria and the support.

lessons.title: Supporting and following up without taking it back
objectives: Use questions before advice when someone you delegated to runs into difficulty.
Decide when taking work back is warranted and how to say so openly.
Give specific credit for delegated work in the places where decisions are made.
Plan a short review with the person of what worked, what to change and what to stop.
lessons.teaching:
The hardest moment in delegation comes when the work gets difficult. A leader who knows how to fix the problem is tempted to step in, and stepping in can feel like support. OPM's 2015 managerial framework describes a different skill: asking questions and continuing to ask them while resisting the impulse to give advice for every situation, grounding observations in behavior and facts, and following up periodically. OPM's 2018 memo on coaching adds a boundary. Coaching serves learning and development and does not replace a supervisor's performance management duties, so a real performance concern goes through the performance process with Human Resources.

Coach before you rescue. Ask what the person has tried, what options they see and what would help. Share what you have noticed in specific terms, and offer a resource or a contact rather than an answer where you can. FEMA's leadership course advises keeping in contact without hovering, since people learn by doing, while you stay responsible for the outcome. Deloitte research by Bernadette Dillon and Juliet Bourke describes empowerment as room to handle difficult situations and decide about one's own work. Take work back only for a real reason, such as risk to people served or a legal deadline, say why plainly and keep the person involved.

Credit is part of the handover. When delegated work goes well, name the person's contribution where it counts: in updates to leadership, in meetings with partners and in the project's own records. Be specific about what they did. Washington State's enterprise leadership competencies list genuine, everyday recognition of people's work as part of developing them. Ask how each person prefers to be recognized, since some would rather have a quiet word than public thanks.

Close the loop with a short review together. Ask what worked, what was harder than expected, what support helped and what was missing. Share your own part, such as where your brief was unclear or a check-in came too late. Then agree on what you will both keep, change or stop, and whether the next piece of work can carry more authority. Every few months, look back privately at the kinds of work you handed over and ask whether development is reaching the whole team, without keeping notes on anyone.
lessons.keyPoint: When delegated work gets hard, coach before you rescue, take work back only for a stated reason, give specific credit where decisions are made, and review together what to keep, change or stop.
lessons.example: Practice case: Ben supervises an eligibility policy team. He asked Dev, an experienced program consultant who is hard of hearing and has run partner meetings for years, to plan a public input session on a rule change. Ten days before the session, Dev tells Ben the venue fell through and two community groups have raised concerns about the agenda. Ben ran sessions like this for years and knows a venue contact. Dev sounds stretched but has not asked Ben to take over.
lessons.question: What should Ben do in his next conversation with Dev?
choices: Ask what Dev has tried and what would help, offer the venue contact, and agree on an earlier check-in before the session date.
Take over the venue and the agenda himself since time is short, and let Dev run the session logistics on the day itself.
Reassure Dev that he trusts him completely, then step back so that Dev can solve it on his own and grow from the whole experience.
feedback: This keeps Dev in charge, adds the help that matters most right now and brings the next check-in forward. Ben supports the work without taking it back.
This may save time, but it takes the visible and difficult parts from Dev at the moment he could learn most, and the community groups lose the contact they had.
Trust matters, but stepping back when someone is stretched leaves them alone with the risk. Support and a closer check-in show trust better than distance does.
lessons.reflection: When someone you hand work to starts to struggle, what do you feel pulled to do, and what would help you ask one more question first?
lessons.action: This week, hold a short review with someone you handed work to: what worked, what was hard and what support helped. Agree on one thing to keep, one to change and the authority for the next piece, and ask yourself who has not yet been offered work like it.

check.question: Someone you delegated to has hit a problem you could solve quickly. What does this lesson suggest you do first?
check.correct: Ask what they have tried and what would help before offering your own answer.
wrong: Solve it quickly yourself, then explain how you did it so they learn the method.
Leave them to work it out alone, since stepping in would undercut their authority.
check.feedback: Questions keep the person in charge of the work and show you what support would actually help. Stepping in or stepping away each removes the coaching that turns delegation into development.

cards.back: Handing over a task with the authority to act and the support to finish it, so the person moves the work without you. You stay accountable for the outcome.
How much the person may decide on their own, from looking into something and reporting back to owning the work fully. Name it when you hand work over.
An agreed time and format for talking about delegated work, plus the signs that should prompt an earlier talk, so neither person is left guessing.
Work designed to stretch someone beyond their current skills so they can meet more complex demands. It needs clear criteria and real support to be fair.
Removing delegated work from the person handling it. Do it only for a stated reason, such as risk to people served, and keep them involved in what remains.

aid.heading: Before you hand it over
items: Sort the task: needs my role, someone could do now, or someone could learn.
Ask who has not yet been offered work like this, and why.
Decide the level of authority that fits the task's risk and the person's experience.
If the work would shift someone into another classification's duties, talk with Human Resources first.

aid.heading: When you hand it over
items: Say what done looks like and who the work serves.
Name the limits: budget, policy, timelines and who else must approve.
State the authority in plain words: report back, recommend, decide and tell me first, decide and update me, or own it fully.
Agree on check-in times, a format that works for the person and what should prompt an earlier call.
Name the support that comes with the work.

aid.heading: While it is underway and after
items: Stay in touch without hovering, and ask what they have tried before giving advice.
Take work back only for a stated reason, and keep the person involved.
Give specific credit in updates, partner meetings and project records.
Review together what to keep, change or stop, and whether the next piece can carry more authority.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Federal Supervisory and Managerial Frameworks and Guidance (September 2015)
sources.note: Adapted from the definition of delegation (tasks, authority, resources and feedback), the objective criteria for delegating, and the coaching objectives on questions before advice. Federal guidance from 2015.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Effective Learning Interventions for Developing ECQs (November 2015)
sources.note: Supports the description of a developmental assignment as work designed to stretch a person beyond existing skills. A 2015 federal literature review built on OPM's earlier leadership competency model.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Coaching in the Federal Government (memorandum, September 10, 2018)
sources.note: Supports the point that coaching is for learning and development and does not replace a supervisor's performance management duties. Federal guidance; state rules come from Minnesota sources.

sources.title: Washington State Department of Enterprise Services — Enterprise Leadership Competencies (2025)
sources.note: Supports the references to giving every employee the chance to develop and to everyday recognition. Another state's competency model, cited for ideas only; Washington presents its indicators as examples, not requirements.

sources.title: Deloitte University Press — Bernadette Dillon and Juliet Bourke, The six signature traits of inclusive leadership (2016)
sources.note: Supports the description of empowerment as room to handle difficult situations and make decisions about one's own work. Consulting research from 2016, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Supports the names of the continuum's orientations used in lesson 3 to describe habits of offering stretch work. Used as shared vocabulary for practices only; no one is assessed or placed on it.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Administrative Procedure 17.1, Work Out of Class Assignments (revised 2024)
sources.note: Supports the description of work out of class assignments as substantially all the duties of a temporarily unoccupied position in another classification, and that labor agreement terms apply. Human Resources advises on any specific assignment.

sources.title: FEMA Emergency Management Institute — IS-240.B Leadership and Influence, Instructor Guide (February 2014)
sources.note: Adapted from the delegation guidance in lesson 6: grant authority that matches the task, keep in contact without hovering, the leader remains responsible for outcomes, and people learn by doing. Federal public-domain training from 2014; the current IS-240.c course (2021) may differ, and completing it does not count toward required training credits.

sources.title: Center for Creative Leadership — The 70-20-10 Rule for Leadership Development (2025)
sources.note: Supports the point that challenging assignments are a main source of leader learning, from CCL's Lessons of Experience research. The 70-20-10 split is a guideline, not a measured law; the research studied managers and executives, and independent critics question its evidence base.
